role.altitude: The captain keeps navigating, signalling other vessels and the crew, and advising masters; writing positions, weather, tank entries and passenger counts into logbooks by hand shrinks.
skills_to_grow: Checking sensor-filled log entries before signing
role.ambitious_version: A captain who signs a complete log at the end of the watch instead of filling it in after the trip.

tasks.short: Watch traffic, agree passing by radio, signal passing vessels with lights, boards or sound signals and note notable encounters in the log.

steps.what: Captain watches traffic on radar, AIS and by eye
Captain agrees the passing with the other vessel by radio
Captain signals passing vessels with lights, the blue board or whistle signals
Captain notes notable encounters in the logbook

tasks.design: Signalling stays fully with the captain. The only change: in an electronic logbook, a notable encounter entry starts with the time, own position and the other vessel's name taken from the navigation system and AIS, and the captain adds what happened.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocked it; signalling is seamanship.
tasks.enabler_now: Electronic logbooks that take entries from navigation data.
tasks.still_hard: Vessels that do not answer the radio.
tasks.human_edge: Reading another skipper's intention from how the ship moves.

reach.learn: Whether logged encounters with position and time help investigations.

evidence.claim: Electronic logbooks fill entries from automation and sensor data and are accepted by the Dutch flag among others.
No AI Act high-risk area applies to log keeping.

assumptions: Boundary: signalling during passing; navigation planning is outside.
Input contract for s4: own position and time from the navigation system and the other vessel's name from AIS, on ships with an electronic logbook.
Watching, radio and signals keep their full time. s4 keeps 70 because time, position and the other vessel's name fill in and the captain still writes what happened.

incremental.description: Captain checks the vessel named in the entry is the right one.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: about half of the fleet keeps paper logbooks, so s4 keeps 85 (0.6); high: an electronic logbook on board (1.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Watch the crew at the ramp or tow, signal crew members or deckhands to rig tow lines, open or close gates or ramps and pull guard chains, check the ramp is closed and log closure times.

steps.what: Captain watches the crew and the situation at the ramp, gate or tow
Captain signals crew members to rig tow lines, open or close ramps and pull guard chains
Captain checks that ramps and gates are closed before departure
Captain writes the ramp and gate closure times in the logbook

tasks.design: Signalling the crew stays fully with the captain. On ferries with door and ramp sensors, the open and closed times are written to the electronic logbook from the ship's automation, and the captain confirms them instead of writing them.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocked it; this is ship handling.
tasks.enabler_now: Ship automation that feeds door and ramp status into electronic logbooks.
tasks.human_edge: Timing the signal to the swell.

evidence.claim: Electronic logbooks fill entries from automation and sensor data.
Logs that record who did what and when need works council consent if used to check crew performance.

assumptions: Boundary: signalling the crew at berths and tows; navigation is outside.
Input contract for s4: door and ramp sensors on ferries feeding the ship's automation and the electronic logbook; tugs without sensors keep writing.
Watching, signalling and checking keep their full time. s4 keeps 40 for confirming the sensor entries and for tugs that keep writing.
unknowns: Whether the vessel has ramp sensors.
research_questions: Do logged closure times match what the crew reports?

incremental.description: No new work: confirming the sensor entries is inside s4.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most of the vessels are tugs without sensors, so s4 keeps 80 (1.0); high: ferries with door and ramp sensors (3.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Have crew enter rest hours, maintain records of positions and movements, weather and water conditions, personnel reports, cargo or passenger status and pollution control entries, and sign the log.

steps.what: Captain records ship positions, movements, distance run and ports of call in the logbook
Captain records weather and water conditions
Crew members enter their hours of work and rest
Captain records crew on board, hours of rest and personnel reports
Captain records cargo or passenger status
Captain records pollution control entries in the oil and garbage record books
Captain reviews and signs the day's log

tasks.design: An electronic logbook approved by the flag state takes position, distance run, times of arrival and departure and wind from the navigation and weather sensors. Crew members enter their own hours of rest in the logbook app, passenger counts come from the ticket gates and cargo figures from the loading documents, and tank levels for the oil record book come from tank sensors. The captain checks and adds remarks, and signs the day's log as today. Logbooks a flag or regime still requires on paper stay on paper.
tasks.previous_blocker: Every value was read off an instrument or document and written by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Electronic logbooks fed by navigation, weather and tank sensors, accepted by the Dutch flag.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which event will matter to an inspector later.
tasks.altitude: Much less writing; the captain still owns and signs the log.

reach.learn: Whether electronic logs arrive at the office the same day.

evidence.claim: Electronic logbooks cover deck, engine and MARPOL logbooks, fill entries from sensor data and are accepted by more than 20 flag states including the Netherlands.
A Dutch gas carrier operator reports 8,000 hours saved across 20 vessels, 14% less paperwork time, from the first wave of logbook automation (vendor case).
Electronic MARPOL record books are allowed when approved by the flag state, with audit logging and backups.
Inland vessels keep one active logbook per craft; electronic logbooks are allowed where put in place.

assumptions: Boundary: keeping the vessel's logs and record books; reporting to authorities is outside.

Input contract for s1 and s2: position, distance, times and wind from the navigation and weather sensors through the ship's network; about 70% of the vessel's logbooks may be electronic under its flag or regime; the rest stay on paper. s1 keeps 40. s2 keeps 60 because sea state and visibility are still observed and written by the captain.
Input contract for s4: rest hours entered by crew members in the app (s3) with about the effort of the paper sheet.
Input contract for s5: passenger counts from the ticket gates on ferries and cargo figures from the terminal's loading documents.
Input contract for s6: tank levels from the tank sensors; garbage hand-overs are still entered by the captain.
Signing the log keeps its full time; crew time is outside the captain's savings.
unknowns: Which logbooks the vessel's flag allows to be electronic.
research_questions: Do log deficiencies found at inspections fall?

already_counted.description: Captain checks sensor-filled entries and corrects wrong values before signing.

incremental.description: Captain keeps the logbook system's backups and audit export as the flag requires.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the flag lets only about a third of the logbooks be electronic, so s1 keeps 75, s2 keeps 80 and s4 to s6 keep 85 (16.0); high: 70% electronic as assumed (35.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Look up current notices for the route, board and brief the master, advise ships' masters on harbour rules and customs procedures, answer their questions and record the pilotage.

steps.what: Pilot looks up current notices to mariners and temporary restrictions for the route
Pilot boards and briefs the master on the passage and harbour rules
Pilot advises ships' masters on harbour rules and customs procedures in answer to their questions
Pilot records the pilotage and advice given in the pilotage report

tasks.design: The pilot's tablet shows the notices and temporary restrictions that touch the planned route, pulled from the harbour master's published notices, instead of the pilot searching them. The pilotage report fills boarding and disembarking times and the track from AIS, and the pilot adds remarks. Briefing and advising the master stay fully with the pilot, as do answers on customs, which come from the pilot's knowledge and the port's published rules.
tasks.previous_blocker: Notices had to be searched per job and reports written after disembarking.
tasks.enabler_now: Published notices to mariners and AIS tracks on pilots' tablets.
tasks.still_hard: Masters who do not speak the pilot's working language well.
tasks.human_edge: Earning a master's trust in the first minutes on the bridge.
tasks.altitude: Little changes; preparation and reporting take a little less time.

reach.learn: Whether route-filtered notices are read before boarding.

evidence.claim: Electronic logbooks and reports can take times and positions from navigation data and AIS.
No AI Act high-risk area applies to advising masters or keeping pilotage reports.

assumptions: Boundary: one pilotage from preparation to report; ship handling is outside.
Input contract for s1: notices published by the harbour master and filtered by the planned route on the tablet; local warnings by radio are still heard on board.
Input contract for s4: AIS track and times for the piloted vessel.
Briefing and advice keep their full time. s4 keeps 70 because times and track fill from AIS and the pilot writes the remarks and advice given.

incremental.description: Pilot checks the AIS times in the report.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many local notices sit outside the route filter (s1 keeps 80) and reports carry long remarks (s4 keeps 85) (4.2); high: the filter and AIS fill work as designed (8.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
